title: Component-Based Out-of-Distribution Detection
claim: Global and local detectors each fail on fine-grained or compositional shifts; decomposing inputs into components catches both.
layout: Stacked rows: example images, success/failure verdict table, score matrices; left-to-right columns
description: A line-drawing figure in three horizontal bands. The top band shows a basket decomposed into labeled parts (handle, rim, body, bottom). Next to it are a rounded ID box with a test basket and an OOD box with two examples: a bucket (fine-grained OOD) and a cup with a basket-like body and a detached handle (compositional OOD). Red and green boxes mark local patches and component regions on each image. The middle band is a table with rows Global, Local and ODBC (the proposed method) and one column per example. Green check marks and red or yellow crosses give each verdict, with short captions such as 'over-sensitive', 'miss detail', 'miss structure' and 'aligned component-level shift'. Dashed red and green arrows link the images to their verdicts. The bottom band has two boxes, CSS and CCS, each holding a small score matrix. The cells that expose the shift are highlighted in green with smiley faces (0.3, 0.6 and 0.2). The eye goes first to the top images, then down to the check and cross table.
caption: Comparison between CoOD and global/local methods. Top: From left to right are: training ID "basket", test ID "basket", fine-grained OOD "bucket", and compositional OOD "cup". Middle: Causes of \green{success} or \red{failure}. Bottom: CSS exposes fine-grained shift in components "bucket's body", while the CCS detects a compositional misalignment in "cup's handle".
abstract: Out-of-Distribution (OOD) detection requires sensitivity to subtle shifts without overreacting to natural In-Distribution (ID) diversity. However, from the viewpoint of detection granularity, global representation inevitably suppress local OOD cues, while patch-based methods are unstable due to entangled spurious-correlation and noise. And neither them is effective in detecting compositional OODs composed of valid ID components. Inspired by recognition-by-components theory, we present a training-free Component-Based OOD Detection (CoOD) framework that addresses the existing limitations by decomposing inputs into functional components. To instantiate CoOD, we derive Component Shift Score (CSS) to detect local appearance shifts, and Compositional Consistency Score (CCS) to identify cross-component compositional inconsistencies. Empirically, CoOD achieves consistent improvements on both coarse- and fine-grained OOD detection.
